The New Testament describes a range of spiritual gifts, among them prophecy, speaking in tongues and their interpretation, healings and miracles, given to believers in the first-century church. Christians agree that the Holy Spirit indwells and gifts every believer today. They disagree about whether these particular gifts were meant only for the apostolic foundation of the church, or whether they continue until Christ returns.

The question became a live debate with the rise of Pentecostalism (1906) and the charismatic renewal, but earlier writers had already reflected on the apparent rarity of such gifts. Three main positions are presented here: cessationism, continuationism, and the mediating 'open but cautious' view, each with its exegesis of key texts, its reading of church history, and its critics' objections and replies.
6567:
Cessationism holds that the miraculous or 'sign' gifts of the Spirit described in the New Testament (especially apostleship, prophecy as new revelation, tongues and their interpretation, and gifts of healing and miracles exercised at will) belonged to the founding era of the church and ceased with the apostles and the completion of the New Testament. God still answers prayer, heals and works providentially, but he no longer distributes revelatory or sign-working gifts to individuals as in the apostolic age.

There are several kinds of cessationist argument. Some (Warfield) emphasise that miracles authenticated the apostles as bearers of revelation. Others (Gaffin) emphasise that prophecy and tongues were revelatory and belonged to the once-for-all foundation of the church, now completed in Scripture. A minority read 'the perfect' of 1 Cor 13:10 as the completed canon; many cessationists, including Gaffin, do not rely on that reading.
